notes.text: God spake all these words — The law of the ten commandments is a law of God's making; a law of his own speaking. God has many ways of speaking to the children of men by his spirit, conscience, providences; his voice in all which we ought carefully to attend to: but he never spake at any time upon any occasion so as he spake the ten commandments, which therefore we ought to hear with the more earnest heed. This law God had given to man before, it was written in his heart by nature; but sin had so defaced that writing, that it was necessary to revive the knowledge of it.

I am the Lord thy God — Herein, God asserts his own authority to enact this law; and proposeth himself as the sole object of that religious worship which is enjoined in the four first commandments. They are here bound to obedience.

1. Because God is the Lord, Jehovah, self-existent, independent, eternal, and the fountain of all being and power; therefore he has an incontestable right to command us.

2. He was their God; a God in covenant with them; their God by their own consent.

He had brought them out of the land of Egypt — Therefore they were bound in gratitude to obey him, because he had brought them out of a grievous slavery into a glorious liberty. By redeeming them, he acquired a farther right to rule them; they owed their service to him, to whom they owed their freedom. And thus, Christ, having rescued us out of the bondage of sin, is entitled to the best service we can do him. The four first commandments, concern our duty to God (commonly called the first-table.) It was fit those should be put first, because man had a Maker to love before he had a neighbour to love, and justice and charity are then only acceptable to God when they flow from the principles of piety.

3. The first commandment is concerning the object of our worship, Jehovah, and him only, Thou shalt have no other gods before me - The Egyptians, and other neighbouring nations, had many gods, creatures of their own fancy. This law was pre-fixed because of that transgression; and Jehovah being the God of Israel, they must entirely cleave to him, and no other, either of their own invention, or borrowed from their neighbours. The sin against this commandment, which we are most in danger of, is giving that glory to any creature which is due to God only. Pride makes a God of ourselves, covetousness makes a God of money, sensuality makes a God of the belly. Whatever is loved, feared, delighted in, or depended on, more than God, that we make a God of. This prohibition includes a precept which is the foundation of the whole law, that we take the Lord for our God, accept him for ours, adore him with humble reverence, and set our affections entirely upon him. There is a reason intimated in the last words before me. It intimates,

1. That we cannot have any other God but he will know it.

2. That it is a sin that dares him to his face, which he cannot, will not, overlook. The second commandment is concerning the ordinances of worship, or the way in which God will be worshipped, which it is fit himself should appoint. Here is,

1. The prohibition; we are forbidden to worship even the true God by images, ver. 4, 5. First, The Jews (at least after the captivity) thought themselves forbidden by this to make any image or picture whatsoever. It is certain it forbids making any image of God, for to whom can we liken him? Isaiah xl, 18, 25. It also forbids us to make images of God in our fancies, as if he were a man as we are. Our religious worship must be governed by the power of faith, not by the power of imagination. Secondly, They must not bow down to them - Shew any sign of honour to them, much less serve them by sacrifice, or any other act of religious worship. When they paid their devotion to the true God, they must not have any image before them for the directing, exciting, or assisting their devotion. Though the worship was designed to terminate in God, it would not please him if it came to him through an image. The best and most ancient lawgivers among the Heathen forbad the setting up of images in their temples. It was forbidden in Rome by Numa a Pagan prince, yet commanded in Rome by the Pope, a Christian bishop. The use of images in the church of Rome, at this day, is so plainly contrary to the letter of this command, that in all their catechisms, which they put into the hand of the people, they leave out this commandment, joining the reason of it to the first, and so the third commandment they call the second, the fourth the third, &c. only to make up the number ten, they divide the tenth into two. For I the Lord Jehovah, thy God, am a jealous God, especially in things of this nature. It intimates the care he has of his own institutions, his displeasure against idolaters, and that he resents every thing in his worship that looks like, or leads to, idolatry: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation - Severely punishing. Nor is it an unrighteous thing with God if the parents died in their iniquity, and the children tread in their steps, when God comes, by his judgments, to reckon with them, to bring into the account the idolatries their fathers were guilty of. Keeping mercy for thousands of persons, thousands of generations, of them that love me and keep my commandments - This intimates, that the second commandment, though in the letter of it is only a prohibition of false worship, yet includes a precept of worshipping God in all those ordinances which he hath instituted. As the first commandment requires the inward worship of love, desire, joy, hope, so this the outward worship of prayer and praise, and solemn attendance on his word. This mercy shall extend to thousands, much further than the wrath threatened to those that hate him, for that reaches but to the third or fourth generation.

7. The third commandment is concerning the manner of our worship; Where we have,

1. A strict prohibition. Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain - Supposing that, having taken Jehovah for their God, they would make mention of his name, this command gives a caution not to mention it in vain, and it is still as needful as ever. We take God's name in vain, First, By hypocrisy, making profession of God's name, but not living up to that profession. Secondly, By covenant breaking. If we make promises to God, and perform not to the Lord our vows, we take his name in vain. Thirdly, By rash swearing, mentioning the name of God, or any of his attributes, in the form of an oath, without any just occasion for it, but to no purpose, or to no good purpose. Fourthly, By false- swearing, which some think is chiefly intended in the letter of the commandment. Fifthly, By using the name of God lightly and carelessly. The profanation of the form of devotion is forbidden, as well as the profanation of the forms of swearing; as also, the profanation of any of those things whereby God makes himself known. For the Lord will not hold him guiltless - Magistrates that punish other offenses, may not think themselves concerned to take notice of this; but God, who is jealous for his honour, will not connive at it. The sinner may perhaps hold himself guiltless, and think there is no harm in it; to obviate which suggestion, the threatening is thus expressed, God will not hold him guiltless - But more is implied, that God will himself be the avenger of those that take his name in vain; and they will find it a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

8. The fourth commandment concerns the time of worship; God is to be served and honoured daily; but one day in seven is to be particularly dedicated to his honour, and spent in his service. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy; in it thou shalt do no manner of work - It is taken for granted that the sabbath was instituted before. We read of God's blessing and sanctifying a seventh day from the beginning, Gen. ii, 3, so that this was not the enacting of a new law, but the reviving of an old law. 1st. They are told what is the day, they must observe, a seventh after six days labour, whether this was the seventh by computation from the first seventh, or from the day of their coming out of Egypt, or both, is not certain. A late pious Writer seems to prove, That the sabbath was changed, when Israel came out of Egypt; which change continued till our Lord rose again: But that then the Original Sabbath was restored. And he makes it highly probable, at least, That the sabbath we observe, is the seventh day from the creation. 2ndly, How it must be observed;

1. As a day of rest; they were to do no manner of work on this day, in their worldly business.

2. As a holy day, set apart to the honour of the holy God, and to be spent in holy exercises. God, by his blessing it, had made it holy; they, by solemn blessing him, must keep it holy, and not alienate it to any other purpose than that for which the difference between it and other days was instituted. 3rdly, Who must observe it? Thou and thy son and thy daughter - The wife is not mentioned, because she is supposed to be one with the husband, and present with him, and if he sanctify the sabbath, it is taken for granted she will join with him; but the rest of the family is instanced in it, children and servants must keep it according to their age and capacity. In this, as in other instances of religion, it is expected that masters of families should take care, not only to serve the Lord themselves, but that their houses also should serve him. Even the proselyted strangers must observe a difference between this day and other days, which, if it laid some restraint upon them then, yet proved a happy indication of God's gracious design, to bring the Gentiles into the church. By the sanctification of the sabbath, the Jews declared that they worshipped the God that made the world, and so distinguished themselves from all other nations, who worshipped gods which they themselves made. God has given us an example of rest after six days work; he rested the seventh day - Took a complacency in himself, and rejoiced in the work of his hand, to teach us on that day, to take a complacency in him, and to give him the glory of his works. The sabbath begun in the finishing of the work of creation; so will the everlasting sabbath in the finishing of the work of providence and redemption; and we observe the weekly sabbath in expectation of that, as well as in remembrance of the former, in both conforming ourselves to him we worship. He hath himself blessed the sabbath day and sanctified it. He hath put an honour upon it; it is holy to the Lord, and honourable; and he hath put blessings into it which he hath encouraged us to expect from him in the religious observation of that day. Let us not profane, dishonour, and level that with common time, which God's blessing hath thus dignified and distinguished.

12. We have here the laws of the second table, as they are commonly called; the six last commandments which concern our duty to ourselves, and one another, and are a comment upon the second great commandment, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. As religion towards God is, an essential branch of universal righteousness, so righteousness towards men is an essential branch of true religion: godliness and honesty must go together. The fifth commandment is concerning the duties we owe to our relations; that of children to their parents is only instanced in, honour thy father and thy mother, which includes,

1. an inward esteem of them, outwardly expressed upon all occasions in our carriage towards them; fear them, Lev. xix, 3, give them reverence, Heb. xii, 9. The contrary to this is mocking at them or despising them,

2. Obedience to their lawful commands; so it is expounded, Eph. vi, 1-3. Children obey your parents; come when they call you, go where they send you, do what they bid you, do not what they forbid you; and this cheerfully, and from a principle of love. Though you have said you will not, yet afterwards repent and obey.

3. Submission to their rebukes, instructions and corrections, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.

4. Disposing of themselves with the advice, direction and consent of parents, not alienating their property, but with their approbation.

5. endeavouring in every thing to be the comfort of their parents, and to make their old age easy to them; maintaining them if they stand in need of support. That thy days may be long in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee - This promise, (which is often literally fulfilled) is expounded in a more general sense Eph. vi, 3. That it may be well with thee, and thou mayst live long on the earth - Those that in conscience towards God keep this and other of God's commandments, may be sure it shall be well with them, and they shall live as long on the earth as infinite wisdom sees good for, them, and what they may seem to be cut short of on earth, shall be abundantly made up in eternal life, the heavenly Canaan which God will give them.

Thou shalt not kill — Thou shalt not do any thing hurtful to the health, or life of thy own body, or any other's. This doth not forbid our own necessary defense, or the magistrates putting offenders to death; but it forbids all malice and hatred to any, for he that hateth his brother is a murderer, and all revenge arising therefrom; likewise anger and hurt said or done, or aimed to be done in a passion; of this our saviour expounds this commandment, Matt. v, 22.
Thou shalt not commit adultery — This commandment forbids all acts of uncleanness, with all those desires, which produce those acts and war against the soul.

Thou shalt not steal — This command forbids us to rob ourselves of what we have, by sinful spending, or of the use and comfort of it by sinful sparing; and to rob others by invading our neighbour's rights, taking his goods, or house, or field, forcibly or clandestinely, over-reaching in bargains, not restoring what is borrowed or found, with-holding just debts, rents or wages; and, which is worst of all, to rob the public in the coin or revenue, or that which is dedicated to the service of religion.

Thou shalt not bear false witness — This forbids,

1. Speaking falsely in any matter, lying, equivocating, and any way devising and designing to deceive our neighbour.

2. Speaking unjustly against our neighbour, to the prejudice of his reputation; And

3. (which is the highest offense of both these kinds put together) Bearing false witness against him, laying to his charge things that he knows not, either upon oath, by which the third commandment, the sixth or eighth, as well as this, are broken, or in common converse, slandering, backbiting, tale-bearing, aggravating what is done amiss, and any way endeavouring to raise our own reputation upon the ruin of our neighbour's.

Thou shalt not covet — The foregoing commands implicitly forbid all desire of doing that which will be an injury to our neighbour, this forbids all inordinate desire of having that which will be a gratification to ourselves. O that such a man's house were mine! such a man's wife mine! such a man's estate mine! This is certainly the language of discontent at our own lot, and envy at our neighbour's, and these are the sins principally forbidden here. God give us all to see our face in the glass of this law, and to lay our hearts under the government of it!
They removed and stood afar off — Before God began to speak, they were thrusting forward to gaze, but now they were effectually cured of their presumption, and taught to keep their distance.

Speak thou with us — Hereby they obliged themselves to acquiesce in the mediation of Moses, they themselves nominating him as a fit person to deal between them and God, and promising to hearken to him as to God's messenger.

Fear not — That is, Think not that this thunder and fire is, designed to consume you. No; it was intended, (1.) To prove them, to try how they could like dealing with God immediately, without a mediator, and so to convince them how admirably well God had chosen for them in putting Moses into that office. Ever since Adam fled upon hearing God's voice in the garden, sinful man could not bear either to speak to God, or hear from him immediately. (2.) To keep them to their duty, and prevent their sinning against God. We must not fear with amazement; but we must always have in our minds a reverence of God's majesty, a dread of his displeasure, and an obedient regard to his sovereign authority.

glossa.text:
*I am the Lord thy God. ((ORIG., hom. 8 in Exod.))* Of him who despises the present world, that is to say Egypt, and, being translated by the word of God, is not found, because he hastens to the world to come, God says: *I am the Lord thy God,* etc. Not to those only who set out from Egypt, but to those who serve the Egyptians no longer, brought out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage ((Psal. LXXX)). The businesses of the world, the acts of the flesh, are the house of bondage: just as to leave the things of the world, and to live according to God, is the house of liberty. Whence John VIII: *If you shall continue in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.* Egypt, therefore, is the house of bondage; Judea and Jerusalem, the house of liberality. As, therefore, earthly Egypt is called for the children of Israel a house of bondage in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which for them is a house of liberty: so, in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of liberty, the whole world and the things that are in it are called a house of bondage: and because from the paradise of liberty men came, through sin, to the bondage of the world, the first word of the decalogue is concerning liberty: *I am the Lord thy God who brought thee out of the land of Egypt,* etc.; this voice thou wilt not be able to hear in Egypt. Even if it be laid upon thee to keep the pasch, to gird thy loins, to take sandals upon thy feet, to hold a rod in thy hand, and to eat unleavened bread with bitterness. But neither in the first station, nor in the second, nor in the third, nor when thou shalt have passed the Red Sea, even if thou come to the sea and the bitterness be turned for thee into sweetness, nor in Elim, where were twelve fountains of waters and seventy palm trees, even if thou pass Raphidim by and climb the remaining stages, art thou yet judged fit, but only when thou shalt have come to Mount Sinai. Scarcely, therefore, wilt thou at some time deserve to receive the precepts of liberty, and to hear: *I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.* This, however, is not the word of a commandment, but it shows who he is that commands. The first commandment, therefore, is: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me.* 

 ((AUG. quaest. in Exod.)) It is asked: how are the ten precepts of the law to be divided? etc., *as far as* unless to that which was said: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me?*

((ISID.)) God gives to Moses the law of our innocence and of the knowledge of himself, which consists in ten words, written on tables of stone by the finger of God. There are three which pertain to the love and the knowledge of the Trinity, seven to the love of one's neighbour, by which human society is not injured. The first pertains to God the Father: *The Lord thy God is one God,* that, hearing this, thou mayest worship one God the Father, and mayest not pour out fornication upon many feigned gods. The second to the Son: *Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain;* that is, do not think that Christ the Son of God is a creature, because every creature is made subject to vanity, but equal to the Father, God of God, light of light.

*Thou shalt not have strange gods,* etc. ((ORIG.)) The first commandment is: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me;* and there follows: *Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness,* etc. Some think all these together to be one commandment: but if it be so reckoned, the number of ten commandments will not be made up. The first commandment, therefore, is: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me,* etc. The second, *Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness,* etc. Let us begin, therefore, from the first commandment: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me.* If he had said, They are not, the statement would seem more absolute; but because he says, *There shall not be,* he did not deny that they are, but forbade that they should be to him to whom these precepts are given. Hence I think Paul took it, I Cor. VIII: *If indeed there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth.* And in other places thou wilt find gods named, as there: *A great king above all gods,* and *God hath spoken to God,* etc. Of lords the same Apostle says: *Whether thrones, or dominations,* etc. ((Col. I.)) But dominations are nothing else than a certain order and multitude of lords. In which the Apostle seems to open the sense of the law; as if he should say: Though there be many lords, who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshipped by others: yet nevertheless there is one God to us, and one Lord. Whence Deut. XXXII: *When the Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam, he appointed the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.* The angels, therefore, to whom the Most High committed the nations, Scripture calls lords or gods: gods as being given by God, and lords as having obtained power from the Lord. Whence it is said to them in psalm LXXXI: *I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the Most High. But you like men shall die, and shall fall like one of the princes;* imitating, that is, the devil, who was made the prince of all unto ruin. Whence it is plain that transgression, not nature, made them accursed. To thee, therefore, O Israel, who art the portion of God and his cord, *there shall not be,* he says, *to thee other gods beside me:* because he who is truly God is one God, and he who is truly Lord is one Lord; but upon the rest, created by himself, he conferred this name not by nature, but by grace. Nor are these things said only to Israel according to the flesh, but rather to thee who hast been made Israel by seeing God in mind, and circumcised in heart, not in flesh; if only thou so act that thou be worthy to be the portion of God, and to be measured in the cord of his inheritance: otherwise let those be an example to thee who had been called to this, that they should be the portion of God, and, their sins requiring it, were scattered through all nations, and, having been brought out of the house of bondage, now serve not the Egyptians alone, but all nations. *For he who sins is the servant of sin ((Joan. V))*.

*Thou shalt not make,* etc. ((ORIG.)) *Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness,* etc. Idols are one thing, gods another. For of gods the Apostle says, I Cor. VIII: *If indeed there are many gods, and many lords,* etc. But of idols, *that an idol is nothing in the world;* of likenesses, however, he did not add that they are nothing. But here it is said: *Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor any likeness whatsoever.* It is one thing, therefore, to make an idol, another to make a likeness. For example, if a man in gold and silver, in wood or in stone, makes the figure of a fourfooted beast, or of a serpent, or of a bird, and sets it up to be adored, he makes not an idol but a likeness. But he who makes what is not, that is, a figure which the eye has not seen but the mind feigns to itself; as if a man should form a dog's head or a ram's upon human limbs, or two faces in the one shape of a man, or the hinder parts of a horse or of a fish upon a human breast; he who does this makes not a likeness, but an idol: for he makes what is not, nor has it anything like itself. Therefore the Apostle says *that an idol is nothing in the world ((I Cor. VIII))*. For no figure is taken from things that subsist, but what an idle and curious mind has invented. But a likeness is when something is formed out of those things which are either in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters: but as it is easy to pronounce concerning the likenesses of those things which are on earth or in the sea, it is not so concerning the heavenly ones; unless one should say that this can be understood of the sun, and the moon, and the stars, whose forms the heathen represent. But Moses, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, desired to forbid also those things which among them were in secret, such as Hecate and the other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls *the spirits of wickedness in the high places*, Ephes. VI; of which perhaps it is said: *My sword is inebriated in heaven ((Isa. XXXIV))*. For by these forms and likenesses they used to invoke demons for the repelling or the avoiding of evils. Yet it must be known that when thou hast resolved to keep this commandment, and to have one God and Lord only, this is to declare war upon all the others, whom thou didst renounce in baptism, confessing God alone, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. But confessing this, unless we love the Lord our God with the whole heart, cleaving to him with the whole soul, with the whole strength, we are not made the portion of the Lord, but, set on the border, we suffer those whom we flee to be offended, and him to whom we flee we do not make favourable. To whom the prophet says: *Woe to the double soul ((Eccli. II))*. And again: *How long do you halt upon both feet? ((III Reg. XVIII.))* From those, then, we are cut down as fugitives, and by our Lord we are not defended as unstable, whence Jer. IV: *Thy lovers are made thine enemies.* Many are the lovers of the soul, taken with her beauty, with whom she has played the harlot, saying: *I will go after my lovers who give me my wine,* etc. ((Ose. II)): these she offends when she returns to her former husband. Unless, therefore, thou remain in whole faith with thy husband, thou art suspect for the crimes which thou hast committed; he marks all thy motions, thy looks and thy goings; he can see nothing further in thee that is wanton, nothing dissolute or prodigal. If, therefore, thou neglect the grace received, and entangle thyself in worldly businesses, straightway the unclean spirit returns with seven others more wicked ((Matth. XII)), that he may not be cast out again, and the last things become worse than the first. There is, then, no fellowship of the temple of God with idols. If we are God's, we ought to be such in whom God may dwell and walk; whence Isa. LII: *You that carry the vessels of the Lord, go out and touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you,* etc. He says, therefore: *There shall not be to thee other gods beside me.*

*Thou shalt not adore,* etc. It is one thing to worship, another to adore. A man can adore unwillingly, either flattering idolatrous kings, or overcome by torments, when he knows that an idol is nothing. But to worship is to be made over wholly to these with affection and zeal. He cuts off both, therefore, that thou mayest neither worship with affection, nor adore in outward show.

*I am the Lord,* etc. See the kindness of God: that he may teach us and make us perfect, he does not refuse the frailty of human affections; he does and suffers all things for our sake, and speaks to us by affections known and familiar to us.


[n: (ORIG., ubi supra.)] Every woman is either under a husband, and is subject to the laws of her husband [n: (Eph. V)], or is a harlot, and uses the liberty of sinning. He who goes in to a harlot knows that he has gone in to one prostituted and open to all, and therefore he cannot [0252D] be indignant about the others. He who uses lawful marriage does not suffer his wife to sin, but is kindled with jealousy to keep the chastity of the marriage, that he may be able to become a lawful father. So every soul is either prostituted with demons, and has many lovers that they may come in to her, now the spirit of fornication, now avarice, and after this will come the spirit of pride and very many others; yet the one does not envy the other, nor is moved with jealous rivalry, but they invite one another in turn; whence, *he brings with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself,* etc. [n: (Luc. XI.)] So the soul that is prostituted to demons suffers no jealous rivalry of her lovers; but if she has been joined to a lawful husband, that is, to Christ, even if at some time she has been a sinner, he does not suffer her to sin further, nor [0253A] can he bear that she should dally with adulterers; his jealousy is stirred up over her, and he defends the chastity of the marriage; but if he sees her violating the rights of the marriage, and seeking an occasion of sinning, he gives her a bill of divorce; whence Isa. L: *For your iniquities has he put away your mother;* and he who speaks this is both jealous and, moved by jealousy, says this. There is also this new kind of his goodness, that he receives her even after adultery when she returns and repents with her whole heart. Whence: *If a woman go out from her husband, and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her own husband?* etc. And elsewhere: *And after thou hast committed fornication in all these things, I said: Return,* etc. [n: (Jer. III.)] Here, therefore, if God being jealous requires and desires thy soul to cleave to him, if he keeps it, rebukes and is indignant, using as it were a certain jealous rivalry [0253B] toward thee, know that there is hope of salvation for thee. But if thou despise the rebuke, his jealousy departs from thee, according to that: *Therefore my jealousy departs from thee,* etc. [n: (Ezech. XVI.)] See the mercy and the loving-kindness of God; when he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and is angry, as he says by Jeremiah: *Thou shalt be chastised with sorrow and with the scourge, O Jerusalem, that my soul depart not from thee [n: (Jer. VI)]*. *For he scourges every son whom he receives [n: (Hebr. XII)]*. But this is a terrible thing, this is the utmost, if we are not rebuked for our sins: for when we exceed the measure of sinning, even the jealousy of God will be taken from us, and he is angry no more.

*Visiting the iniquity,* etc. [n: (ORIG.)] Rendering the sins of the fathers upon the sons, etc. The heretics say that it is not the word of a good God, who says that one is punished [0253C] for the sins of another; yet they say that the God of the law is just, and they cannot show how he is unjust [cj: *injustus*; read *justus*, "how he is just"], if he punishes one when another sins. But our inward man is said either to have God for father, if he lives according to God; or the devil, if he does his will; whence John VIII: *You are of your father the devil, and you will do the desires of your father.* As, therefore, the seed of God is in us, when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin, according to that of I John III, *He who is of God sins not, because the seed of God abides in him;* so when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed; when we do what he persuades, he has now begotten us, for we are born his sons through sin. But because we scarcely ever sin without a helper, as no one commits adultery alone, it is necessary that a partner in the adultery be made, [0253D] and if not more, it is necessary that some man or woman be joined to the service of the crime: all of whom, as it were one from another, begotten according to the order of the persuasion, draw their offspring from the devil; as in the betraying of the Lord the devil entered into the heart of Judas, and begot the first son of sin, who could not do this alone; he went therefore to the Scribes and the Pharisees and the chief priests; there is born, therefore, from Judas a third and a fourth generation of sin. Let us see, therefore, how God renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons unto the third and the fourth generation, and not upon the man himself. For of the fathers nothing is said. The devil, therefore, because he has already exceeded the measure of sinning, like a garment clotted in blood, will not be clean in this world; he is not scourged [0254A] for sin; for all things are kept for him unto the future. whence Matth. VIII): *Why art thou come to torment us before the time?* But the sins are rendered upon the sons whom he has begotten through sin, who, being set in the flesh, are scourged. *God wills not the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live [n: (Ezech. XXXIII)]*. Mercifully, therefore, he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons, because the devil and his angels, who are also made the fathers of sin, are unworthy to be rebuked in the present: their sons, and those who through them have been taken into the fellowship of sin, receive in the present what they have done, that, being purged, they may not be made partners with the devil in punishment. Whence in psalm LXXXVIII: *I will visit their iniquities with a rod,* etc., *but my mercy I will not take away from them.* [var: Vulg. Ps 88:34 *misericordiam autem meam non dispergam ab eo*, "but my mercy I will not scatter away from him"; Migne's plural is what carries the argument to the sons] For God is [0254B] jealous, and the soul which he betroths to himself in faith he wills not to remain in the defilement of sin, but to be quickly purged. But if she will not be purged, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them, Matth. XXV: *Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire,* etc. Let us know, therefore, that we are rebuked in the present, that in the future we may rest. Whence: *When we are chastised, we are rebuked by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world.*

[n: (ID.)] In this saying the heretics are wont to reproach us, that it is not the word of a good God, who judges one for the sins of another. But those who shall say that the God of the law who commands these things is not good, yet call him just: nor indeed can they themselves show how it should seem agreeable to justice if, when one sins, another is punished.

[0254C] [n: (ISID.)] The first commandment forbids stealthy deceit; the second, error; the third slays the love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, cruelty; the sixth, fornication; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth destroys falsehood; the ninth, the coveting of the world; the tenth, the thought of adultery. And it is to be noted that as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the tables are written with ten precepts, by which the people of God may be ruled and the demons slain. For the law was written on two tables that the two Testaments might be signified: or because there are two precepts of love, of God and of one's neighbour, *on which the whole law hangs, and the prophets [n: (Matth. XXII)]*. For on the one are three precepts, which pertain to the love of God; on the other seven, which pertain to the fellowship of one's neighbour. But the tables were [0254D] of stone, because the heart of the Jews was stony and unfeeling, hard and dull; whence Ezech. XXXVI: *I will take away the stony heart, and will give them a heart of flesh.* And the Apostle says [n: (II Cor. III)]: *Not in tables of stone, but in the fleshly tables of the heart,* which, that is, may perceive and understand.

*Honour thy father,* etc. This is the first of the seven commandments which pertain to one's neighbour. And rightly are they seven. For the number seven consists of three and four. And three befits the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible and rational. Four, the body.

*Thou shalt not kill,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 61 in Exod.)) And as to what was said: *thou shalt not kill,* it is not to be thought that anything is done against this precept in that the law kills, or that God commands someone to be killed: for he does it who commands what it is not lawful for the minister to refuse.

*Thou shalt not commit adultery.* ((ISID.)) It is also asked: how does *thou shalt not commit adultery* differ from that which is said a little after: *Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife?* For in that which was said, *thou shalt not commit adultery,* that also could be understood; unless perhaps in those two precepts of not committing adultery and not stealing the deeds themselves are marked, but in these last the very concupiscence: which differ so far, that sometimes a man commits adultery who does not covet his neighbour's wife, when he is joined to her for some other cause. But sometimes he covets, and is not joined to her, fearing punishment: and this perhaps the law wished to show, that both are sins.

((ID.)) Again it is wont to be asked whether under the name of adultery fornication also is held, etc., *as far as* and the unlawful use of those members ought to be understood to be forbidden.

*Thou shalt not steal,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 71 in Exod.)) But again it is asked how *thou shalt not steal* differs from that which is said a little after concerning the not coveting of a neighbour's goods? Not that everyone who covets his neighbour's goods steals; but everyone who steals covets his neighbour's goods. In that generality, where it is enjoined not to covet a neighbour's goods, that also which pertains to theft could have been contained.
*Thou shalt not speak against thy neighbour,* etc. ((AUG., ubi supra. )) In that also which was said, etc., *as far as* and things of this sort.

*And all the people saw the voices,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 72 in Exod.)) It is wont to be asked how the people saw a voice, since a voice seems to pertain not to sight but to hearing, etc., *as far as* hear what shines, we are not accustomed to say.

*Speak thou to us,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 73.)) It is signified that fear pertains rather to the Old Testament, as love to the New; although in the Old the New lies hidden, and in the New the Old lies open. But how it can be granted to such a people to see the voice of God, if this is to be taken as understanding, since they fear that God should speak to them lest they die, is not sufficiently clear.

*Fear not,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 74.)) Thus they were to be restrained from sins, by fearing, that is, lest they should suffer sensible punishments; because they were not yet able to love justice, and they were tempted by the Lord, that it might appear of what sort they were; not that they might become known to God whatever sort they were, from whom nothing was hidden, but that they might become known among themselves and to their own selves.

notes.text: The heavens — They are as a legible book, wherein he that runs may read it. The glory - His eternal power and Godhead, his infinite wisdom and goodness. Firmament - Or, the expansion, all the vast space extended from the earth to the highest heavens, with all its goodly furniture.

Day — Every day and night repeats these demonstrations of God's glory. Uttereth - Or, poureth forth, constantly and abundantly, as a fountain doth water; So this Hebrew word signifies. Knowledge - Gives us a clear knowledge or discovery of God their author.

Heard — Or, understood; there are divers nations in the world, which have several languages, so that one cannot discourse with, or be understood by another, but the heavens are such an universal teacher, that they can speak to all people, and be clearly understood by all.

Line — Their lines, the singular number being put for the plural. And this expression is very proper, because the heavens do not teach men audibly, or by speaking to their ears, but visibly by propounding things to their eyes, which is done in lines or writings. Gone - Is spread abroad. Earth - So as to be seen and read, by all the inhabitants of the earth. Words - Their magnificent structure, their exquisite order, and most regular course, by which they declare their author, no less than men discover their minds by their words. Sun - Which being the most illustrious and useful of all the heavenly bodies, is here particularly mentioned.

Bridegroom — Gloriously adorned with light as with a beautiful garment, and smiling upon the world with a pleasant countenance. Chamber - In which he is poetically supposed to have rested all night, and thence to break forth as it were on a sudden. Strong man - Conscious and confident of his own strength.
The ends — His course is constant from east to west, and thence to the east again. So that there is no part of the earth which doth not one time or other feel the benefit of his light and heat.

The law — The doctrine delivered to his church, whether by Moses, or by other prophets. Having discoursed hitherto of the glory of God shining forth in, the visible heavens, he now proceeds to another demonstration of God's glory, which he compares with and prefers before the former. Perfect - Completely discovering both the nature and will of God, and the whole duty of man, what he is to believe and practice, and whatsoever is necessary to his present and eternal happiness. Whereas the creation, although it did declare so much of God, as left all men without excuse, yet did not fully manifest the will of God, nor bring men to eternal salvation. Converting - From sin to God, from whom all men are naturally revolted. Testimony - His law, so called because it is a witness between God and man, what God requires of man, and what upon the performance of that condition, he will do for man. Sure - Hebrew. faithful or true, which is most necessary in a witness: it will not mislead any man, but will infallibly bring him to happiness. Simple - Even persons of the lowest capacities.

Right — Both in themselves, and in their effect, as guiding men in the ready way to eternal happiness. Rejoicing - By the discoveries of God's love to sinful men, in offers and promises of mercy. Commandment - All his commands. Pure - Without the least mixture of error. The eyes - Of the mind, with a compleat manifestation of God's will and man's duty: both which, the works of nature, and all the writings of men discover but darkly and imperfectly.

The fear — The law and word of God, because it is both the object and the rule, and the cause of holy fear. Clean - Sincere, not adulterated with any mixture. Constant and unchangeable, the same for substance in all ages. Judgments - God's laws are frequently called his judgments, because they are the declarations of his righteous will, and as it were his judicial sentence by which he expects that men should govern themselves, and by which he will judge them at the last day.

Who — Thy law, O Lord, is holy and just and good. But I fall infinitely short of it. Cleanse - Both by justification, through the blood of thy son; and by sanctification thro' thy Holy Spirit. Though the first may seem to be principally intended, because he speaks of his past sins. Secret - From the guilt of such sins as were secret either, from others; such as none knows but God and my own conscience: or, from myself; such as I never observed, or did not discern the evil of. Pardon my unknown sins, of which I never repented particularly, as I should have done.

Presumptuous — From known and evident sins, such as are committed against knowledge, against the checks of conscience, and the motions of God's spirit. Dominion - If I be at any time tempted to such sins, Lord let them not prevail over me, and if I do fall into them, let me speedily rise again.

Let — Having prayed that God would keep him from sinful actions, he now prays that God would govern, and sanctify his words and thoughts: and this was necessary to preserve him from presumptuous sins, which have their first rise in the thoughts. Redeemer - This expression seems to be added emphatically, and with special respect to Christ, to whom alone this word Goel can properly belong. A prayer for the king, ver. 1-4. The king and the people rejoice in God, and pray for his help, ver. 5-9. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The heavens shew forth. ((Ibid.))* First, speaking of the incarnation, he commends the preaching of the new law. ((AUG.)) The heavens, the apostles, concerning the glory of Christ in which he is equal to the Father. ((CASS.)) Or the heavens, they who sent the star. *The glory. ((Ibid.))*: That God freely forgives sins. *The works.* ((AUG.)) Those which are according to man, etc., *as far as* and these same are made night to him, giving to the darkened the knowledge which is of things human. ((CASS.)) And this so wonderfully, that it is in all tongues; and so widely, that it is in every part of the compass of the earth.

*Day unto day.* ((CASS.)) He treats of it by demonstration. ((AUG.)) *Day unto day.* The Spirit brings forth to spiritual men the fullness of wisdom, etc., *as far as* this teaching is continued by days and by nights down to those who come after.

*Speeches.* ((CASS.)) Public persuadings. *Words.* Common narrations. *Whose voices are not heard.* He would say more plainly, in whom their voices are not heard, or, the voices of all their words are heard: he does the same thing by means of the relative.

((AUG.)) The Spirit made the first men speak with all tongues, he who was to gather all nations into one; then one man was for all, so now one Christ, head and body.

*In the sun* ((CASS.)) What he praises others for having done, he himself does: he preaches the incarnation. Or in the sun, in the open sight of the world, or in labour. The sun burns, and shines, and varies the seasons. *His tabernacle.* ((AUG.)) As it were a soldier's dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to storm the errors of the world. Or the tabernacle, the Church in the open, not in secret, so as to lie hid. *A bridegroom.* ((CASS.)) So often promised by the prophets, a great likeness of the sacrament: therefore born of a virgin, that he might join to himself the Church a virgin. *Out of his bride-chamber.* ((AUG.)) That is, the virginal womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Behold, humble in mercy, but strong in majesty. *As a giant to run.* ((CASS.)) Unshaken, not to be called back, overcoming human nature by his power. *From the highest.* Here the Trinity is shewn, etc., *as far as* it marks the unity of the Trinity. *Neither is there any that can hide himself,* etc. ((AUG.)) The Word made flesh permitted no man to excuse himself out of the shadow of death: because the heat of the Word pierced even that. Or, the heat is the Spirit, whom he sent when he had returned, who is law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear and judgments, because he does these things.

*The law of the Lord.* ((CAS.)) Secondly, he praises the precepts of the New and the Old Testament. ((Ibid.)) The law given through Moses, correcting all things by the distinction of its words, and sending them on to the grace of Christ. *Converting.* ((AUG.)) By liberty, unto the imitating of himself, not pressing down with the yoke of servitude. *Souls.* Wills, not merely hands, as the Old Testament did. *The testimony.* Whatsoever *Quaecunquae* testimonies he gave to Israel are full of truth, and have given wisdom to the humble. *Wisdom:* concerning things divine.

*The justices of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* All are right in him, who taught not what he did not do, so that they who imitate them might rejoice in them, seeing they would do them freely with charity, not slavishly with fear. ((CASS.)) *Justices,* the law which justifies; whatsoever it commands is just.

*The fear of the Lord. ((Ibid.))* The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not profitable, and it changes with the times. *The fear of the Lord* is without any perturbation, because it is a love mingled with dread, because if it fears the judge, it knows him merciful. ((AUG.)) Fear, not that penal fear for earthly things, for love of which the soul is afraid, but the chaste fear whereby, the more it loves, the more it is wary of offending the bridegroom, and therefore it is not cast out, but abides. *Judgments.* The judgments of God need not another's authority.

*Desirable things. ((Ibid.))* Or, much to be desired, or much gold and stone; or much that is precious. Desirable above gold, etc., *as far as,* whose will he sets before his own, and they are sweeter than he himself is to himself. *Above gold,* that is, everything that is sought after, whether for riches, or for power, or for pleasure. *Honey.* The food of God is honey; that is, one now loosed from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, because he is still wrapped about, for whom there is need of the pressure of God's hand squeezing him out, that he may go into life.

*Who understandeth sins. ((Ibid.))* Thirdly he asks to be purged of vices, that he may be a worthy psalmist, to report these sacraments. To a mind that sees, truth is sweet, and judgments sweet; to one that does not see, what sweetness is there? But why is it not seen? Because of sins: nor is it any wonder: *For who understandeth sins?* ((CASS.)) *Sins:* all of them, for certain of them are known. *Mine* defile, *others'* afflict, and now spare, drive back the persuader. *From my secret ones.* He includes all sins under two heads, etc., *as far as* whereby man was seduced; and by consenting he made it his own. ((AUG.)) There is no greater sin than to apostatize from God, which is the beginning of pride: but pride is the beginning and the cause of all sin.

notes.text: Though I — He subjoins this in the singular number, because the Philippians could not say thus.

Circumcised the eighth day — Not at ripe age, as a proselyte. Of the tribe of Benjamin - Sprung from the wife, not the handmaid. An Hebrew of Hebrews - By both my parents; in everything, nation, religion, language. Touching the law, a pharisee - One of that sect who most accurately observe it.
Having such a zeal for it as to persecute to the death those who did not observe it. Touching the righteousness which is described and enjoined by the Law — That is, external observances, blameless.
But all these things, which I then accounted gain, which were once my confidence, my glory, and joy, those, ever since I have believed, I have accounted loss, nothing worth in comparison of Christ.

Yea, I still account both all these and all things else to be mere loss, compared to the inward, experimental knowledge of Christ, as my Lord, as my prophet, priest, and king, as teaching me wisdom, atoning for my sins, and reigning in my heart. To refer this to justification only, is miserably to pervert the whole scope of the words. They manifestly relate to sanctification also; yea, to that chiefly. For whom I have actually suffered the loss of all things — Which the world loves, esteems, or admires; of which I am so far from repenting, that I still account them but dung - The discourse rises. Loss is sustained with patience, but dung is cast away with abhorrence. The Greek word signifies any, the vilest refuse of things, the dross of metals, the dregs of liquors, the excrements of animals, the most worthless scraps of meat, the basest offals, fit only for dogs. That I may gain Christ - He that loses all things, not excepting himself, gains Christ, and is gained by Christ. And still there is more; which even St. Paul speaks of his having not yet gained.

And be found by God ingrafted in him, not having my own righteousness, which is of the law — That merely outward righteousness prescribed by the law, and performed by my own strength. But that inward righteousness which is through faith - Which can flow from no other fountain. The righteousness which is from God - From his almighty Spirit, not by my own strength, but by faith alone. Here also the apostle is far from speaking of justification only.

The knowledge of Christ, mentioned in the eighth verse, is here more largely explained. That I may know him — As my complete saviour. And the power of his resurrection - Raising me from the death of sin, into all the life of love. And the fellowship of his sufferings - Being crucified with him. And made conformable to his death - So as to be dead to all things here below.
The resurrection of the dead — That is, the resurrection to glory.

Not that I have already attained — The prize. He here enters on a new set of metaphors, taken from a race. But observe how, in the utmost fervour, he retains his sobriety of spirit. Or am already perfected - There is a difference between one that is perfect, and one that is perfected. The one is fitted for the race, ver. 15; the other, ready to receive the prize. But I pursue, if I may apprehend that - Perfect holiness, preparatory to glory. For, in order to which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus - Appearing to me in the way, Acts xxvi, 14. The speaking conditionally both here and in the preceding verse, implies no uncertainty, but only the difficulty of attaining.
I do not account myself to have apprehended this already; to be already possessed of perfect holiness.

Forgetting the things that are behind — Even that part of the race which is already run. And reaching forth unto - Literally, stretched out over the things that are before - Pursuing with the whole bent and vigour of my soul, perfect holiness and eternal glory. In Christ Jesus - The author and finisher of every good thing.

glossa.text: *Although I also,* etc. Lest the Apostle should seem to despise in others what he himself does not have, and not to be able to trust in the flesh, he subjoins: *Although,* etc.

*Of the tribe of Benjamin.* The tribe of Benjamin clave to Judah, not departing from the temple, when the separation was made under the servant of Solomon. For then the tribe of Judah, which was royal, and the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Levi, which was priestly, remained together, not departing from Jerusalem and from the temple.
*For Christ.* Lest I should show the coming of Christ either not yet accomplished, or to be superfluous. For all these hindrances were empty things, that one might not come to grace.

*Nevertheless I esteem.* Not only for the sake of having Christ have I so judged, but even if I could not attain him. *For* this alone, namely for the *knowledge* which we have of Jesus, *pre-eminent,* above the other kinds of knowledge. *As dung.* As if: Not only the losses of goods, but the things which defile one who is now observing them: and this to this end, that in the future they may have Christ for their reward: and that here I may be a member in him: which cannot come about otherwise unless I esteem those things as dung.

*My own righteousness,* etc. If righteousness is from the law, how is it thine? Didst thou impose the law upon thyself? God gave the law and imposed it. God commanded thee to obey his law. But it is also thine, because thou presumest upon the law, reckoning that by thine own will thou canst fulfil the law.

((CHRYS.)) Rightly did he say: *Not having my own righteousness,* etc., *as far as* which have proceeded from our own zeal.

*But that,* etc. ((AUG.)) Which obtains from God, which takes away fear, etc., *as far as* it is wholly to be taken away according to the shadow of the figures of the law. *Righteousness in faith.* That is, righteousness is a thing existing in faith, and as it was born of faith, so it has no being save in faith.

*Unto the knowing.* He subjoins the commendation of faith, by the many things which it does. For it makes us know God perfectly in the other life also, who here is believed. And to have the resurrection, which our resurrection is the power and efficacy of the resurrection of Christ And in this life to have fellowship in suffering: for unless through faith, no man would suffer so great things; and the conformation of [his] death, that is, that we may die, as he did, if there be need.

*I may meet.* Rendering to God the things which he has bestowed on me, and by this coming to the resurrection. Or, I may meet Christ in the judgment, which belongs to the saints only, coming first to the true and glorious resurrection, which is not among the dead, but far out of the dead: because, although all rise again on the day of judgment, yet the just alone shall be gloriously changed, and shall meet the Lord in the air, borne up by angels. But the ungodly shall remain on the earth until they receive the terrible sentence of the judge.

*Not that I have already received.* This he says of himself, lest those whom he praises should be exalted as men, but should add labour, as he himself does who is so great. *But I follow after,* etc. Not with the steps of the body, but with the affections of the mind and the manners of life, that I may be able to be a perfect possessor of righteousness: I who, advancing by a straight road from day to day by spiritual renewal, am already a perfect wayfarer of that same righteousness. For he was a perfect wayfarer, but not yet one arrived by the perfection of the journey itself. *If by any means I may comprehend.* This he says because it is difficult. And lest it should seem superfluous to suffer so many things, since he has faith and the other good things, he subjoins: Deservedly do I labour so much for that glory, because I do *Not* say that I have *already received* anything: for if I have received anything of glory, it is nothing in comparison with what is to come. *Or* if I have received anything, as concerning the knowledge of Christ, I do not say that in it *I am perfect.* And if it is thus of me. what of me who of others?
*The things which are behind.* His former deeds, not because they were evil, but small toward merit, but stretched out toward the better things, that he may always advance unto what is better.
*I press on.* Even so far, until I come to the appointed good. *Of the supernal vocation.* That is, of eternal life, unto which God calls, and therefore it is a worthy thing, etc.

notes.text: A certain householder planted a vineyard — God planted the Church in Canaan; and hedged it round about - First with the law, then with his peculiar providence: and digged a wine press - Perhaps it may mean Jerusalem: and built a tower - The temple: and went into a far country - That is, left the keepers of his vineyard, in some measure, to behave as they should see good. Mark xii, 1; Luke xx, 9.
He sent his servants — His extraordinary messengers, the prophets: to the husbandmen - The ordinary preachers or ministers of the Jews.
They say — Perhaps some of the by-standers, not the chief priests or Pharisees; who, as St. Luke relates, said, God forbid, Luke xx, 16.

The builders — The scribes and priests, whose office it was to build up the Church. Is become the head of the corner - Or the chief corner stone: he is become the foundation of the Church, on which the whole building rests, and is the principal corner stone, for uniting the Gentiles to it, as the chief corner stone of a house supports and links its two sides together. Psalm cxviii, 22.
Therefore — Because ye reject this corner stone. The kingdom of God - That is, the Gospel.

Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken — Stumblers at Christ shall even then receive much hurt. He is said to fall on this stone, who hears the Gospel and does not believe. But on whomsoever it shall fall - In vengeance, it will utterly destroy him. It will fall on every unbeliever, when Christ cometh in the clouds of heaven. Luke xx, 18.

glossa.text: *A vineyard.* Of which Isaias ((cap. IV)). *The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth,* etc. *He dug in it a winepress.* By the digging fear is marked, because they kept those commandments of the law not out of love but out of fear.
*When the time of the fruits drew nigh,* etc. Rightly the time of the fruits, not of the fruit: because there was none in that stubborn people.
*Last of all,* etc. See the patience of the father of the household, who waits for repentance. *They will reverence.* As though, I shall do what is mine, let them see to what is theirs.

*This is the heir.* It is plain that the chief priests killed Jesus not through ignorance but through envy, since they knew him to be the one to whom it is said: *Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance ((Psal. II))*; whence also, taking counsel for themselves, they said: *If we let him alone so ((Joan. II))*, etc. *We shall have his inheritance.* The inheritance of Christ, which he possessed in rising again, is the Church, which the Jews were striving to snatch away: while, his faith being put out, they endeavoured to persuade the Gentiles of the justice that is of the law.

*They cast him forth out of the vineyard.* Mark changes this order, saying: *They killed him and cast him forth out of the vineyard ((Luc. XX))*, as a worthless corpse. In which he marks their obstinacy, because when the Lord had been killed and raised again, they shut him out from their own borders and sent him to the Gentiles.

*The builders.* Who seemed to be building a house for God, as it were, out of the people subject to them.

*And he that shall fall,* etc. He who believes and yet sins: the stone falls upon him and he is not ground to powder, but he is bound tight, because through patience he is kept for salvation; but he upon whom the stone rushes down, that is, he who denies, is utterly ground to powder, so that not even a shard remains; or it falls upon him who now despises and does injuries, and he has not yet utterly perished, but is shaken so that he does not walk upright. The stone falls upon him when, coming in judgment, it crushes him, when he says: *Go into everlasting fire.*

echoes.text: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.
echoes.note: 'Circumcised the eighth day' directly invokes the Abrahamic covenant statute that every male be circumcised at eight days old. Paul cites his impeccable conformity to this Torah marker as the leading item of fleshly 'confidence' he renounces. High volume and verbal precision.

echoes.text: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy.
echoes.note: 'As to zeal, persecuting the church' casts Paul in the line of Phinehas, whose 'zeal' (LXX zelos) for God by violent action averted wrath and won a covenant of priesthood. Paul reads his pre-Christian persecuting as this paradigmatic zeal, now reassessed as loss. Strong thematic coherence; 'zeal' is the operative catchword.

echoes.text: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: The legal restatement 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised' reinforces the same eighth-day statute Paul claims. A secondary witness to the precept behind his pedigree.

echoes.text: As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin.
echoes.note: 'Of the tribe of Benjamin' points to Rachel's son Benjamin, named at Genesis 35:18; Paul's tribal claim asserts descent from a fully Israelite, non-proselyte lineage. Identity-marker allusion rather than verbal quotation.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's 'I have been very zealous for the LORD' supplies the second exemplar of biblical zeal that frames Paul's self-description as a zealot-persecutor. The Phinehas–Elijah zeal tradition was a live Second-Temple ideal, available to Paul.

echoes.text: Phinehas our father, for that he was zealous exceedingly, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
echoes.note: Mattathias's deathbed roll names 'Phinehas our father, because he was zealous with great zeal,' the proximate Second-Temple charter for the violent-zeal ideal Paul embodied as persecutor. Availability within the deuterocanon and thematic fit are strong; included as a Maccabean development of the zeal motif.

echoes.text: He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
echoes.note: 'Of the stock of Israel' evokes the renaming of Jacob as Israel, the patronym of the chosen people Paul claims as his birthright. Faint background to the ethnic boast.

echoes.text: And he was zealous for the law, even as Phinehas did to Zimri the son of Salu.
echoes.note: Mattathias acts 'as Phinehas did,' showing 'zeal for the law' expressed in killing apostates — precisely the persecuting zeal Paul claims and renounces. Faint, supplementary to 1 Macc 2:54.

echoes.text: Then Phinehas stood up, and executed judgment, so the plague was stopped. That was credited to him for righteousness, for all generations to come.
echoes.note: The Psalter reckons Phinehas's intervention to him 'as righteousness' forever; Paul's pairing of zealous persecution with 'righteousness in the law, blameless' may trade on this Phinehas-righteousness link. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'That I may know him' and the renunciation of every fleshly ground of boasting answers Jeremiah's oracle: let no one boast in wisdom, might, or riches, but only that 'he understands and knows me, the LORD.' Paul transmutes covenant 'knowledge of God' into 'the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.' Strong coherence and Pauline recurrence (cf. 1 Cor 1:31).

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The righteousness which is from God by faith,' set against the law's righteousness, restates Paul's governing text 'the righteous shall live by faith' (cf. Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). The faith/law antithesis here is the same justification doctrine Habakkuk anchors.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: Righteousness 'from God by faith' rather than 'of my own from the law' is the Abrahamic credo 'he believed the LORD, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,' Paul's standard proof that righteousness is faith-reckoned, not works-earned. High coherence with Pauline usage.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'If by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead' depends on Daniel's promise that 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake,' the principal OT text for bodily resurrection. Paul's hope of out-resurrection presupposes this Danielic apocalyptic frame. High availability and coherence.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
echoes.note: 'Let us know, let us press on to know the LORD... on the third day he will raise us up' links 'knowing' God to resurrection — exactly Paul's sequence of 'know him and the power of his resurrection.' The verbal pairing of knowledge and rising is distinctive.

echoes.text: No weapon that is formed against you will prevail; and you will condemn every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of Yahweh, and their righteousness which is of me,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is from me, says the LORD' is a Septuagintal source for a 'righteousness from God' that is gift, not achievement — Paul's exact phrase. Verbal overlap with 'righteousness from God' supports the echo.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live; the dwellers in the dust shall awake and sing' is the prophetic companion to Daniel 12 for resurrection hope, undergirding Paul's 'resurrection from the dead.' Recurrence of the resurrection motif strengthens the link.

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: The martyrs' confidence that 'the King of the world will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life' is the Second-Temple development of resurrection hope Paul shares. Faint and supplementary to Daniel, so contested.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.
echoes.note: The Servant 'set his face' and is vindicated by God who 'justifies' him; Paul's 'fellowship of his sufferings... conformed to his death' followed by resurrection vindication may echo the suffering-then-vindicated Servant pattern. Faint, figural.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.
echoes.note: 'Pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD' offers a Septuagintal background of pressing/pursuing after a goal that resonates with Paul's 'I press on toward the goal.' Faint, athletic-pursuit imagery is widespread.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Seek peace and pursue it' supplies the verb of strenuous pursuit Paul reuses in 'I press on/pursue toward the goal.' One of several possible Septuagintal sources for the diolko motif, hence contested.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The parable's setup (21:33) reproduces the Song of the Vineyard almost verbatim from Isaiah 5:2 (LXX): a man planted a vineyard, set a hedge/fence about it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. The whole parable presupposes Isaiah's allegory of the vineyard as Israel/Judah and its expected fruit.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.
echoes.note: Jesus cites Psalm 118:22-23 verbatim (21:42): 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner. This was from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' interpreting the rejected/vindicated son as the rejected/exalted cornerstone (same Psalm 118 quoted at the entry, 21:9).

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: 21:44, 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust,' draws on Daniel's stone cut without hands that smashes the kingdoms and whose fragments become chaff blown away — the stone that both judges and inaugurates God's kingdom.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' on which many 'shall fall, and be broken' supplies the first half of 21:44 ('he who falls on this stone will be broken'), fusing with the Psalm 118 cornerstone into a composite stone-testimonium.

echoes.text: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
echoes.note: The tenants' deliberation, 'This is the heir. Come, let's kill him, and seize his inheritance' (21:38), closely echoes Joseph's brothers: 'Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now, let us kill him' — the heir/beloved son plotted against by his own.

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: 'I sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them, yet they did not listen' (cf. Jer 25:4) is the prophetic pattern behind the householder repeatedly sending servants who are beaten and killed (21:34-36).

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, sent by God to the people, was stoned to death in the court of the temple — a concrete instance of a divine messenger stoned, matching 'stoned another' (21:35).

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel's confession that 'they slew your prophets which testified against them to turn them to you' summarizes the rejected-and-killed-emissaries pattern the parable allegorizes.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine brought out of Egypt and planted, whose hedges God then breaks down so passers-by pluck it, is a second vineyard-as-Israel song reinforcing Isaiah 5 and the threat to remove the vineyard's protection (21:43).

echoes.text: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.
echoes.note: 'The LORD testified against Israel... by all the prophets... yet they would not hear, but hardened their necks' — the deuteronomistic summary of prophets sent and rejected, paralleling the servants' fate.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'precious cornerstone' laid in Zion as a sure foundation belongs to the same stone-testimonia cluster (with Ps 118:22) that early Christians combined to interpret Christ as the cornerstone.

echoes.text: Yahweh will enter into judgment with the elders of his people, and their leaders: “It is you who have eaten up the vineyard. The plunder of the poor is in your houses.
echoes.note: 'You have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses' — Israel's leaders arraigned for plundering the vineyard, resonant with the tenants who seize the produce and inheritance.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd' as the divinely sent figure who is struck may faintly inform the killing of the beloved son, though the imagery differs.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to 'a nation producing its fruit' (21:43) faintly recalls Daniel's everlasting kingdom given to the people of the saints, the transfer of dominion to a faithful nation.
