notes.text: Now — I will record it to be a witness for God, and against you, as Moses did his song, Deut. xxxi, 19; xxxii, 1. To - To the Lord of the vineyard. Of my beloved - Not devised by me, but inspired by God. Vineyard - His church. Hill - Hills being places most commodious for vines.
He gathered — He removed all hindrances, and gave them all the means of fruitfulness. A tower - For the residence of the keepers.

Nor digged — Vine-dressers use to dig up and open the earth about the roots of the vines. The meaning is, I will remove my ministers, who used great care and diligence to make you fruitful. Thorns - I will give you up to your own lusts. No rain - I will deprive you of all my blessings.
Pleasant — In whom God formerly delighted. A cry - From the oppressed, crying to men for help, and to God for vengeance.

glossa.text: *I will sing to my beloved,* etc. ((HIER.)) A canticle is sometimes in gladness, sometimes in sorrow, as this one is, namely the one which he composed who, seeing the city, wept, saying: *For if thou also hadst known,* etc. ((Luc. XIX)).

*A chosen vineyard.* ((ID.)) Another edition, the vineyard Sorec, which is a kind of the best vine, most fruitful with unfailing fruits; all the things that are said of the vineyard are referred to the state of the soul, which, planted by God, brought forth not grapes but wild grapes: and it was handed over to the beasts to be trodden down, nor did it receive the rain of doctrine, because it despised the gifts that had gone before.
*Now therefore, O inhabitants,* etc. In like manner Nathan questions David, that he may pronounce sentence upon himself as though upon another.
*Is it that I looked for,* etc.? This, according to some, he said above within himself; but here he asks others what he had been thinking.

*And now I will show you.* As if he should say: Because you will not answer, therefore I will answer for you.

 *I will take away,* etc. That is, that they who have not felt God through benefits may feel him through punishments; and therefore he threatens a penalty, that they may be turned to repentance.
*And the clouds.* ((ID.)) Which under Elias, etc., *as far as* when they had not the prophets, and drove the apostles away.

*The house of Israel,* etc. ((ID.)) From the time the kingdom was divided, etc., *as far as* because Christ was born of them.

*Behold a cry.* Wherewith it cried out against the Lord and shouted, saying: Away with him, away with him, crucify him; or, they made a cry in place of justice, because they slew Christ, whose blood cries to the Lord: *The voice of the blood sanguis of thy brother Abel crieth to me from the earth ((Gen. IV))*.

notes.text: Preparedst — Thou didst root out the idolatrous nations. Deep root - Thou gavest them a firm settlement.
The hills — They filled not only the fruitful valleys, but even the barren mountains.
The river — They possessed the whole land, from the mid-land sea to the river Euphrates.
Hedges — Taken away thy protection.

glossa.text: *O God of hosts.* ((AUG.)) It is the way of one who desires, to repeat often what he prays for with such prayers.

*A vineyard.* ((CASS.)) Of the vineyard, how it was begun, and perfected. ((AUG. et CASS.)) *A vineyard out of Egypt,* as if to say, we shall be saved, but thou wilt destroy the Jews, for whom thou didst so much: and that not for a light fault, but because they did not know the coming of Christ. Or, we shall be saved because thou hast so foreshown it. *A vineyard out of Egypt.* But why wilt thou destroy? this is of the unbelieving. *Out of Egypt.* As he cast out those men from Egypt, so he cast the Church out of the darkness of vices: he *plants* the Gentiles in virtues, and *leads* them through this desert of the world. *The roots,* he makes the martyrs and others firm, and fills the world. ((CASS.)) *A vineyard out of Egypt,* through mystical figures, etc., *as far as* which has been so spread abroad through the world. *A guide,* while he leads her by a spiritual journey. *The roots,* the prophets, the Apostles, the martyrs and others, from whom, stretching out her *branches,* she takes and covers the world. *A guide of the way.* ((AUG.)) Or another reading, etc., *as far as* and it is not another, but the same vineyard: thence the Apostles, thence also the other just men, although some branches were broken off.

*It covered* ((CASS.)) The height and the breadth of the vineyard are here set forth. The vineyard is from above, which overshadows even the loftier mountains with life and doctrine, and makes them grow great. Vines that climb trees are called *bushes,* by which the lesser ones in the Church are understood. *Cedars,* not the proud, but those that are *God's,* are the martyrs, who are high in the Church, and these too the Church protects in her bosom. *The shoots,* the sons of regeneration, who flowed from the river Jordan, because there the rule of baptism began. *The mountains.* ((AUG.)) The prophets, etc., *as far as* likewise *they cover the cedars of God,* that is, the doctors. *The cedars of God.* ((ID.)) Because there are cedars to be overthrown, namely the proud, who are the cedars of the world, but not of God.

*Why.* He wonders why the defence of the Lord was withdrawn from such a one as this. ((AUG.)) *Why.* Because she was proud against the planter, and slew the servants sent to her, and at last the son and heir, the fence was destroyed, and the nations found her destroyed, and blotted her out. This Asaph first bewails, but not without hope: for he speaks now of those who direct their heart.

*The boar.* ((AUG. et CASS.)) Vespasian, strong and savage, and hostile to the Jews, who among other creatures hold this beast unclean. *A singular wild beast.* Titus, who consumed the remnant with a terrible devouring, who is called *singular,* that is, proud. Or the boar and the *wild beast* are taken for the same thing, namely the Roman army. And see by what sins man labours and perishes. *Singular.* ((AUG.)) Every proud man says: *I am, I am, and there is none other. The boar.* ((CASS.)) The devil, strong and fierce, *out of the wood,* because his thoughts are wild and trackless. *But thou, O Lord God of hosts.* Or continue it thus: So the vineyard was laid waste, but that the remnant may be saved, *O God of hosts, turn again,* and at the end of the last age serenely *behold,* he prays this remedy for those changed for the better.

*And perfect thou that which thy right hand hath planted.* ((AUG.)) Set up no other, but perfect this one. For in this is the seed of Abraham: there is the root that bears the wild olive. Perfect it, *because blindness in part has happened in Israel, that the fulness of the Gentiles might come in, and so all Israel should be saved ((Rom. XII))* . *Upon the son.* ((CASS.)) Founded upon and *et*; read *te*, "thee", etc., *as far as* but of the fire of good love it is said: *I am come to send fire on the earth, and what will I, but that it burn? ((Luc. XII.))*

notes.text: Though I — He subjoins this in the singular number, because the Philippians could not say thus.

Circumcised the eighth day — Not at ripe age, as a proselyte. Of the tribe of Benjamin - Sprung from the wife, not the handmaid. An Hebrew of Hebrews - By both my parents; in everything, nation, religion, language. Touching the law, a pharisee - One of that sect who most accurately observe it.
Having such a zeal for it as to persecute to the death those who did not observe it. Touching the righteousness which is described and enjoined by the Law — That is, external observances, blameless.
But all these things, which I then accounted gain, which were once my confidence, my glory, and joy, those, ever since I have believed, I have accounted loss, nothing worth in comparison of Christ.

Yea, I still account both all these and all things else to be mere loss, compared to the inward, experimental knowledge of Christ, as my Lord, as my prophet, priest, and king, as teaching me wisdom, atoning for my sins, and reigning in my heart. To refer this to justification only, is miserably to pervert the whole scope of the words. They manifestly relate to sanctification also; yea, to that chiefly. For whom I have actually suffered the loss of all things — Which the world loves, esteems, or admires; of which I am so far from repenting, that I still account them but dung - The discourse rises. Loss is sustained with patience, but dung is cast away with abhorrence. The Greek word signifies any, the vilest refuse of things, the dross of metals, the dregs of liquors, the excrements of animals, the most worthless scraps of meat, the basest offals, fit only for dogs. That I may gain Christ - He that loses all things, not excepting himself, gains Christ, and is gained by Christ. And still there is more; which even St. Paul speaks of his having not yet gained.

And be found by God ingrafted in him, not having my own righteousness, which is of the law — That merely outward righteousness prescribed by the law, and performed by my own strength. But that inward righteousness which is through faith - Which can flow from no other fountain. The righteousness which is from God - From his almighty Spirit, not by my own strength, but by faith alone. Here also the apostle is far from speaking of justification only.

The knowledge of Christ, mentioned in the eighth verse, is here more largely explained. That I may know him — As my complete saviour. And the power of his resurrection - Raising me from the death of sin, into all the life of love. And the fellowship of his sufferings - Being crucified with him. And made conformable to his death - So as to be dead to all things here below.
The resurrection of the dead — That is, the resurrection to glory.

Not that I have already attained — The prize. He here enters on a new set of metaphors, taken from a race. But observe how, in the utmost fervour, he retains his sobriety of spirit. Or am already perfected - There is a difference between one that is perfect, and one that is perfected. The one is fitted for the race, ver. 15; the other, ready to receive the prize. But I pursue, if I may apprehend that - Perfect holiness, preparatory to glory. For, in order to which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus - Appearing to me in the way, Acts xxvi, 14. The speaking conditionally both here and in the preceding verse, implies no uncertainty, but only the difficulty of attaining.
I do not account myself to have apprehended this already; to be already possessed of perfect holiness.

Forgetting the things that are behind — Even that part of the race which is already run. And reaching forth unto - Literally, stretched out over the things that are before - Pursuing with the whole bent and vigour of my soul, perfect holiness and eternal glory. In Christ Jesus - The author and finisher of every good thing.

glossa.text: *Although I also,* etc. Lest the Apostle should seem to despise in others what he himself does not have, and not to be able to trust in the flesh, he subjoins: *Although,* etc.

*Of the tribe of Benjamin.* The tribe of Benjamin clave to Judah, not departing from the temple, when the separation was made under the servant of Solomon. For then the tribe of Judah, which was royal, and the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Levi, which was priestly, remained together, not departing from Jerusalem and from the temple.
*For Christ.* Lest I should show the coming of Christ either not yet accomplished, or to be superfluous. For all these hindrances were empty things, that one might not come to grace.

*Nevertheless I esteem.* Not only for the sake of having Christ have I so judged, but even if I could not attain him. *For* this alone, namely for the *knowledge* which we have of Jesus, *pre-eminent,* above the other kinds of knowledge. *As dung.* As if: Not only the losses of goods, but the things which defile one who is now observing them: and this to this end, that in the future they may have Christ for their reward: and that here I may be a member in him: which cannot come about otherwise unless I esteem those things as dung.

*My own righteousness,* etc. If righteousness is from the law, how is it thine? Didst thou impose the law upon thyself? God gave the law and imposed it. God commanded thee to obey his law. But it is also thine, because thou presumest upon the law, reckoning that by thine own will thou canst fulfil the law.

((CHRYS.)) Rightly did he say: *Not having my own righteousness,* etc., *as far as* which have proceeded from our own zeal.

*But that,* etc. ((AUG.)) Which obtains from God, which takes away fear, etc., *as far as* it is wholly to be taken away according to the shadow of the figures of the law. *Righteousness in faith.* That is, righteousness is a thing existing in faith, and as it was born of faith, so it has no being save in faith.

*Unto the knowing.* He subjoins the commendation of faith, by the many things which it does. For it makes us know God perfectly in the other life also, who here is believed. And to have the resurrection, which our resurrection is the power and efficacy of the resurrection of Christ And in this life to have fellowship in suffering: for unless through faith, no man would suffer so great things; and the conformation of [his] death, that is, that we may die, as he did, if there be need.

*I may meet.* Rendering to God the things which he has bestowed on me, and by this coming to the resurrection. Or, I may meet Christ in the judgment, which belongs to the saints only, coming first to the true and glorious resurrection, which is not among the dead, but far out of the dead: because, although all rise again on the day of judgment, yet the just alone shall be gloriously changed, and shall meet the Lord in the air, borne up by angels. But the ungodly shall remain on the earth until they receive the terrible sentence of the judge.

*Not that I have already received.* This he says of himself, lest those whom he praises should be exalted as men, but should add labour, as he himself does who is so great. *But I follow after,* etc. Not with the steps of the body, but with the affections of the mind and the manners of life, that I may be able to be a perfect possessor of righteousness: I who, advancing by a straight road from day to day by spiritual renewal, am already a perfect wayfarer of that same righteousness. For he was a perfect wayfarer, but not yet one arrived by the perfection of the journey itself. *If by any means I may comprehend.* This he says because it is difficult. And lest it should seem superfluous to suffer so many things, since he has faith and the other good things, he subjoins: Deservedly do I labour so much for that glory, because I do *Not* say that I have *already received* anything: for if I have received anything of glory, it is nothing in comparison with what is to come. *Or* if I have received anything, as concerning the knowledge of Christ, I do not say that in it *I am perfect.* And if it is thus of me. what of me who of others?
*The things which are behind.* His former deeds, not because they were evil, but small toward merit, but stretched out toward the better things, that he may always advance unto what is better.
*I press on.* Even so far, until I come to the appointed good. *Of the supernal vocation.* That is, of eternal life, unto which God calls, and therefore it is a worthy thing, etc.

notes.text: A certain householder planted a vineyard — God planted the Church in Canaan; and hedged it round about - First with the law, then with his peculiar providence: and digged a wine press - Perhaps it may mean Jerusalem: and built a tower - The temple: and went into a far country - That is, left the keepers of his vineyard, in some measure, to behave as they should see good. Mark xii, 1; Luke xx, 9.
He sent his servants — His extraordinary messengers, the prophets: to the husbandmen - The ordinary preachers or ministers of the Jews.
They say — Perhaps some of the by-standers, not the chief priests or Pharisees; who, as St. Luke relates, said, God forbid, Luke xx, 16.

The builders — The scribes and priests, whose office it was to build up the Church. Is become the head of the corner - Or the chief corner stone: he is become the foundation of the Church, on which the whole building rests, and is the principal corner stone, for uniting the Gentiles to it, as the chief corner stone of a house supports and links its two sides together. Psalm cxviii, 22.
Therefore — Because ye reject this corner stone. The kingdom of God - That is, the Gospel.

Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken — Stumblers at Christ shall even then receive much hurt. He is said to fall on this stone, who hears the Gospel and does not believe. But on whomsoever it shall fall - In vengeance, it will utterly destroy him. It will fall on every unbeliever, when Christ cometh in the clouds of heaven. Luke xx, 18.

glossa.text: *A vineyard.* Of which Isaias ((cap. IV)). *The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth,* etc. *He dug in it a winepress.* By the digging fear is marked, because they kept those commandments of the law not out of love but out of fear.
*When the time of the fruits drew nigh,* etc. Rightly the time of the fruits, not of the fruit: because there was none in that stubborn people.
*Last of all,* etc. See the patience of the father of the household, who waits for repentance. *They will reverence.* As though, I shall do what is mine, let them see to what is theirs.

*This is the heir.* It is plain that the chief priests killed Jesus not through ignorance but through envy, since they knew him to be the one to whom it is said: *Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thine inheritance ((Psal. II))*; whence also, taking counsel for themselves, they said: *If we let him alone so ((Joan. II))*, etc. *We shall have his inheritance.* The inheritance of Christ, which he possessed in rising again, is the Church, which the Jews were striving to snatch away: while, his faith being put out, they endeavoured to persuade the Gentiles of the justice that is of the law.

*They cast him forth out of the vineyard.* Mark changes this order, saying: *They killed him and cast him forth out of the vineyard ((Luc. XX))*, as a worthless corpse. In which he marks their obstinacy, because when the Lord had been killed and raised again, they shut him out from their own borders and sent him to the Gentiles.

*The builders.* Who seemed to be building a house for God, as it were, out of the people subject to them.

*And he that shall fall,* etc. He who believes and yet sins: the stone falls upon him and he is not ground to powder, but he is bound tight, because through patience he is kept for salvation; but he upon whom the stone rushes down, that is, he who denies, is utterly ground to powder, so that not even a shard remains; or it falls upon him who now despises and does injuries, and he has not yet utterly perished, but is shaken so that he does not walk upright. The stone falls upon him when, coming in judgment, it crushes him, when he says: *Go into everlasting fire.*

echoes.text: He who is eight days old will be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations, he who is born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your seed.
echoes.note: 'Circumcised the eighth day' directly invokes the Abrahamic covenant statute that every male be circumcised at eight days old. Paul cites his impeccable conformity to this Torah marker as the leading item of fleshly 'confidence' he renounces. High volume and verbal precision.

echoes.text: “Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them, so that I didn’t consume the children of Israel in my jealousy.
echoes.note: 'As to zeal, persecuting the church' casts Paul in the line of Phinehas, whose 'zeal' (LXX zelos) for God by violent action averted wrath and won a covenant of priesthood. Paul reads his pre-Christian persecuting as this paradigmatic zeal, now reassessed as loss. Strong thematic coherence; 'zeal' is the operative catchword.

echoes.text: In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
echoes.note: The legal restatement 'on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised' reinforces the same eighth-day statute Paul claims. A secondary witness to the precept behind his pedigree.

echoes.text: As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin.
echoes.note: 'Of the tribe of Benjamin' points to Rachel's son Benjamin, named at Genesis 35:18; Paul's tribal claim asserts descent from a fully Israelite, non-proselyte lineage. Identity-marker allusion rather than verbal quotation.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's 'I have been very zealous for the LORD' supplies the second exemplar of biblical zeal that frames Paul's self-description as a zealot-persecutor. The Phinehas–Elijah zeal tradition was a live Second-Temple ideal, available to Paul.

echoes.text: Phinehas our father, for that he was zealous exceedingly, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.
echoes.note: Mattathias's deathbed roll names 'Phinehas our father, because he was zealous with great zeal,' the proximate Second-Temple charter for the violent-zeal ideal Paul embodied as persecutor. Availability within the deuterocanon and thematic fit are strong; included as a Maccabean development of the zeal motif.

echoes.text: He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
echoes.note: 'Of the stock of Israel' evokes the renaming of Jacob as Israel, the patronym of the chosen people Paul claims as his birthright. Faint background to the ethnic boast.

echoes.text: And he was zealous for the law, even as Phinehas did to Zimri the son of Salu.
echoes.note: Mattathias acts 'as Phinehas did,' showing 'zeal for the law' expressed in killing apostates — precisely the persecuting zeal Paul claims and renounces. Faint, supplementary to 1 Macc 2:54.

echoes.text: Then Phinehas stood up, and executed judgment, so the plague was stopped. That was credited to him for righteousness, for all generations to come.
echoes.note: The Psalter reckons Phinehas's intervention to him 'as righteousness' forever; Paul's pairing of zealous persecution with 'righteousness in the law, blameless' may trade on this Phinehas-righteousness link. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'That I may know him' and the renunciation of every fleshly ground of boasting answers Jeremiah's oracle: let no one boast in wisdom, might, or riches, but only that 'he understands and knows me, the LORD.' Paul transmutes covenant 'knowledge of God' into 'the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.' Strong coherence and Pauline recurrence (cf. 1 Cor 1:31).

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'The righteousness which is from God by faith,' set against the law's righteousness, restates Paul's governing text 'the righteous shall live by faith' (cf. Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). The faith/law antithesis here is the same justification doctrine Habakkuk anchors.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: Righteousness 'from God by faith' rather than 'of my own from the law' is the Abrahamic credo 'he believed the LORD, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,' Paul's standard proof that righteousness is faith-reckoned, not works-earned. High coherence with Pauline usage.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: 'If by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead' depends on Daniel's promise that 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake,' the principal OT text for bodily resurrection. Paul's hope of out-resurrection presupposes this Danielic apocalyptic frame. High availability and coherence.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let us acknowledge Yahweh. Let us press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.”
echoes.note: 'Let us know, let us press on to know the LORD... on the third day he will raise us up' links 'knowing' God to resurrection — exactly Paul's sequence of 'know him and the power of his resurrection.' The verbal pairing of knowledge and rising is distinctive.

echoes.text: No weapon that is formed against you will prevail; and you will condemn every tongue that rises against you in judgment. This is the heritage of the servants of Yahweh, and their righteousness which is of me,” says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is from me, says the LORD' is a Septuagintal source for a 'righteousness from God' that is gift, not achievement — Paul's exact phrase. Verbal overlap with 'righteousness from God' supports the echo.

echoes.text: Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust; for your dew is like the dew of herbs, and the earth will cast out the departed spirits.
echoes.note: 'Your dead shall live; the dwellers in the dust shall awake and sing' is the prophetic companion to Daniel 12 for resurrection hope, undergirding Paul's 'resurrection from the dead.' Recurrence of the resurrection motif strengthens the link.

echoes.text: And when he was at the last gasp, he said, You, miscreant, do release us out of this present life, but the King of the world shall raise up us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal renewal of life.
echoes.note: The martyrs' confidence that 'the King of the world will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life' is the Second-Temple development of resurrection hope Paul shares. Faint and supplementary to Daniel, so contested.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed. He is near who justifies me; who will bring charges against me? Let us stand up together: who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord Yahweh will help me; who is he who shall condemn me? Behold, all they shall wax old as a garment, the moth shall eat them up.
echoes.note: The Servant 'set his face' and is vindicated by God who 'justifies' him; Paul's 'fellowship of his sufferings... conformed to his death' followed by resurrection vindication may echo the suffering-then-vindicated Servant pattern. Faint, figural.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from.
echoes.note: 'Pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD' offers a Septuagintal background of pressing/pursuing after a goal that resonates with Paul's 'I press on toward the goal.' Faint, athletic-pursuit imagery is widespread.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Seek peace and pursue it' supplies the verb of strenuous pursuit Paul reuses in 'I press on/pursue toward the goal.' One of several possible Septuagintal sources for the diolko motif, hence contested.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The parable's setup (21:33) reproduces the Song of the Vineyard almost verbatim from Isaiah 5:2 (LXX): a man planted a vineyard, set a hedge/fence about it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. The whole parable presupposes Isaiah's allegory of the vineyard as Israel/Judah and its expected fruit.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This is Yahweh’s doing. It is marvelous in our eyes.
echoes.note: Jesus cites Psalm 118:22-23 verbatim (21:42): 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same was made the head of the corner. This was from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' interpreting the rejected/vindicated son as the rejected/exalted cornerstone (same Psalm 118 quoted at the entry, 21:9).

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: 21:44, 'He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust,' draws on Daniel's stone cut without hands that smashes the kingdoms and whose fragments become chaff blown away — the stone that both judges and inaugurates God's kingdom.

echoes.text: He will be a sanctuary, but for both houses of Israel, he will be a trap and a snare for the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many will stumble over it, fall, be broken, be snared, and be captured.”
echoes.note: Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling and rock of offense' on which many 'shall fall, and be broken' supplies the first half of 21:44 ('he who falls on this stone will be broken'), fusing with the Psalm 118 cornerstone into a composite stone-testimonium.

echoes.text: They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. They said one to another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
echoes.note: The tenants' deliberation, 'This is the heir. Come, let's kill him, and seize his inheritance' (21:38), closely echoes Joseph's brothers: 'Behold, this dreamer comes. Come now, let us kill him' — the heir/beloved son plotted against by his own.

echoes.text: Since the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt to this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them: yet they didn’t listen to me, nor inclined their ear, but made their neck stiff: they did worse than their fathers.
echoes.note: 'I sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them, yet they did not listen' (cf. Jer 25:4) is the prophetic pattern behind the householder repeatedly sending servants who are beaten and killed (21:34-36).

echoes.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’” They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
echoes.note: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, sent by God to the people, was stoned to death in the court of the temple — a concrete instance of a divine messenger stoned, matching 'stoned another' (21:35).

echoes.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient, and rebelled against you, and cast your law behind their back, and killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
echoes.note: Israel's confession that 'they slew your prophets which testified against them to turn them to you' summarizes the rejected-and-killed-emissaries pattern the parable allegorizes.

echoes.text: You brought a vine out of Egypt. You drove out the nations, and planted it. You cleared the ground for it. It took deep root, and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shadow. Its boughs were like God’s cedars. It sent out its branches to the sea, Its shoots to the River. Why have you broken down its walls, so that all those who pass by the way pluck it? The boar out of the wood ravages it. The wild animals of the field feed on it. Turn […]
echoes.note: The vine brought out of Egypt and planted, whose hedges God then breaks down so passers-by pluck it, is a second vineyard-as-Israel song reinforcing Isaiah 5 and the threat to remove the vineyard's protection (21:43).

echoes.text: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.
echoes.note: 'The LORD testified against Israel... by all the prophets... yet they would not hear, but hardened their necks' — the deuteronomistic summary of prophets sent and rejected, paralleling the servants' fate.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'precious cornerstone' laid in Zion as a sure foundation belongs to the same stone-testimonia cluster (with Ps 118:22) that early Christians combined to interpret Christ as the cornerstone.

echoes.text: Yahweh will enter into judgment with the elders of his people, and their leaders: “It is you who have eaten up the vineyard. The plunder of the poor is in your houses.
echoes.note: 'You have eaten up the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses' — Israel's leaders arraigned for plundering the vineyard, resonant with the tenants who seize the produce and inheritance.

echoes.text: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is close to me,” says Yahweh of Armies. “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will turn my hand against the little ones.
echoes.note: 'Strike the shepherd' as the divinely sent figure who is struck may faintly inform the killing of the beloved son, though the imagery differs.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The kingdom given to 'a nation producing its fruit' (21:43) faintly recalls Daniel's everlasting kingdom given to the people of the saints, the transfer of dominion to a faithful nation.

turn.trap: Becomes flat anti-Jewish caricature (indicting a whole people rather than a specific leadership's specific choice) or bare Christology-trivia (identify the stone, move on) — missing that the parable indicts anyone entrusted with a vineyard who starts treating the produce as their own.
turn.hinge: The tenants' plan is chillingly rational — "this is the heir; let us kill him and have his inheritance" — the murder isn't rage, it's a business calculation. The horror is how reasonable it sounds from inside the wrong premise.

doors.claim: Hedge, tower, winepress — the tenants inherited an estate they didn't build, and forgot that before the first rent was ever due.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: He hath 'planted' a vine of which Isaiah speaks, 'The vine of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel.' And 'hedged it round about.'

witnesses.author: Rabanus Maurus
witnesses.reading: Morally; a vineyard has been let out to each of us to dress, when the mystery of baptism was given us, to be cultivated by action.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: God planted the Church in Canaan; and hedged it round about — first with the law, then with his peculiar providence: and went into a far country — that is, left the keepers of his vineyard, in some measure, to behave as they should see good.

doors.say: Nothing you're standing on was built by you — the hedge and the tower were already there before you showed up to work.
doors.do: Have them name one thing in their life or ministry they've started treating as self-made rather than received.

doors.claim: The murder is coldly reasoned — kill the heir, keep the inheritance — which is scarier than a crime of passion, because it means clear thinking got them there.

witnesses.author: Rabanus Maurus
witnesses.reading: The Jews endeavoured by putting Him to death to seize upon the inheritance, when they strove to overthrow the faith which is through Him.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Wherefore then did He not send Him immediately? That from what they had done to the others they might accuse themselves.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: It is plain that the chief priests killed Jesus not through ignorance but through envy.

doors.say: Sin rarely announces itself as sin — it usually shows up as the reasonable next step from a premise nobody questioned.
doors.do: Ask them to name a decision that felt perfectly rational but started from a false premise about what actually belongs to them.

doors.landing: The stone that breaks or grinds
doors.claim: There's no neutral way to meet the rejected stone — you're either broken open by it, and can be healed, or you try to grind it down and are ground to powder instead.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: Those that fall upon Him, are those that despise and afflict Him. These do not perish utterly, but are broken so that they walk not upright.

witnesses.author: Pseudo-Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: It is one thing to be broken, and another to be ground to powder. Of what is broken there remains something; but what is ground to powder is as it were converted into dust.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He who believes and yet sins: the stone falls upon him and he is not ground to powder, but he is bound tight, because through patience he is kept for salvation; but he upon whom the stone rushes down, that is, he who denies, is utterly ground to powder.

doors.say: You cannot stay neutral toward the rejected stone — either it breaks you in a way you can recover from, or you try to break it and there's nothing left of you.
doors.do: Ask them which posture they're currently in toward something Christ has asked of them: broken open, or grinding against it.

doors.landing: What more could I have done?
doors.claim: Isaiah's song is a lament of love: God has done everything for this vineyard, and grieves over what it became.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: A canticle is sometimes in gladness, sometimes in sorrow, as this one is, namely the one which he composed who, seeing the city, wept.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He gathered — he removed all hindrances, and gave them all the means of fruitfulness.

doors.say: This is a love song before it is a judgment. God is not angry at a stranger's field. God is grieving over his own.
doors.do: Ask them to name what God has planted in their life and to thank God for it before asking what it has yielded.

doors.claim: The song traps its hearers the way Nathan trapped David: they judge the vineyard, and discover they have judged themselves.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: In like manner Nathan questions David, that he may pronounce sentence upon himself as though upon another.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: A cry — from the oppressed, crying to men for help, and to God for vengeance.

doors.say: Isaiah lets you condemn the bad vineyard first. Then he tells you whose vineyard it is.
doors.do: Have them find out whose cry is going unheard in their own community, and bring one concrete response to it.

complementary.gravity: Isaiah sings a love song about a vineyard given every care that yielded only wild grapes: God looked for justice and found bloodshed, for righteousness and heard a cry (Isaiah 5). The Psalm begs God to return and tend the vine he brought out of Egypt; Paul counts every credential as loss for Christ (Philippians 3); and Jesus tells of tenants who kill the heir to keep the vineyard. The nerve: God has given everything, and looks for the fruit of justice.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah's vineyard receives every care and yields wild grapes, and God hears a cry where he looked for justice (Isaiah 5); the Psalm pleads for God to tend the vine again (Psalm 80); Paul lets go of every advantage he earned (Philippians 3); and the tenants kill the son to keep what was only lent to them (Matthew 21). Each reading holds a gift up against its fruit and asks what has become of what God entrusted.
synthesis.claim: Everything we have was planted by God; the fruit God looks for is justice and righteousness, not a claim of ownership.
synthesis.here: For a congregation comfortable in an inherited vineyard — buildings, endowments, a good name — the move is Isaiah's question turned on itself: what fruit does God find here, and who is crying out nearby?

semicontinuous.gravity: God gives the Ten Words at Sinai — commands meant to order a free people, not shackle them (Exodus 20); Paul, credentials in hand, counts them all as loss for the sake of knowing Christ (Philippians 3); and Jesus tells of tenants who beat, kill, and finally murder the son sent to collect fruit that was never theirs to withhold. The nerve: everything in the vineyard — the hedge, the tower, the winepress — was gift, on loan, and the tenants' whole crime is forgetting that.

synthesis.convergence: The commandments at Sinai order a people who did not create their own freedom (Exodus 20); Paul discards every credential he actually earned to be found in Christ instead (Philippians 3); and the tenants forget, calculate, and finally kill rather than admit the vineyard was never theirs. Every reading names the same temptation: mistaking what you were given for what you made, then defending the mistake past all reason.
synthesis.claim: Whatever you're protecting as yours was on loan the whole time — the only question is whether you find that out from the owner or from a broken stone.
synthesis.here: For people or institutions confusing stewardship with ownership, don't moralize about greed in the abstract — name the specific gift they've started treating as an entitlement, and ask what rent is actually due.

turn.subtract: Three landings — the forgotten gift, the cold calculation, or the two ways to meet the stone. Choose one.
